awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of an Online Biometric Data Collection Technology
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project investigates the commercial potential of an online biometrics data collection system. Using a webcam, the system collects biomarkers of cognitive effort and attention (heart rate and eye tracking) and emotions (facial electromyography (EMG)). This new solution has many potential applications, including the promotion of message effectiveness for content creators/advertisers. It also has the potential to enhance online training and education activities across education levels and disciplines. The system takes advantage of the naturally occurring signals produced by the body to help content creators and designers understand, in part, what is occurring in the brains of those watching messages using webcam technology.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of an online tool designed to replicate the vectors of biometrics / psychophysiological data typically collected in a fixed lab location, thereby replicating the rigor of traditional in-lab biometric / psychophysiological research without the constraints of geography, time, expense, and heterogeneity. Data collection occurs via browser-based experiments with remote participants, typically yielding message effectiveness results within 24 hours. A user-friendly dashboard visualizes insights, thereby helping content creators refine creative assets quickly. Compared to traditional methods, the approach is roughly 90% faster, significantly cheaper, and easily scaled to a variety of audiences.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Generative artificial intelligence has made it easy to create convincing fake faces, voices, and videos, known as “deepfakes.” Criminals now use these tools to open fraudulent accounts and obtain loans under false or synthetic identities. Industry analysts at Deloitte’s Center for Financial Services project that deepfake-enabled fraud losses could exceed $40 billion by 2027. This I-Corps project explored whether a biometrics-based technology developed by our team, which detects deepfakes by analyzing true human signals of liveness, could become a viable commercial product for protecting lenders and their customers.

The team included Eric Rasmussen (Entrepreneurial Lead), a media psychologist and professor at Texas Tech University; Alison Bryant (Technical Lead), a researcher and executive with deep experience in biometrics and media research; and Daniel Green (Industry Mentor), a fintech executive specializing in highly regulated financial markets. Over the course of the program, the team conducted 100 customer discovery interviews with lenders, loan management system (LMS) providers, identity verification companies, and fraud prevention professionals.

The interviews substantially changed our understanding of the market. We began with a broad target, all online consumer lenders and lending platforms, and a general value proposition built on being instant, passive, and frictionless. Through discovery, we learned that our most promising early customers are risk managers, chief operating officers, and heads of product at online subprime to near-prime lenders. We also learned that LMS providers are a critical channel: when a detection tool integrates with an LMS platform, every lender using that platform becomes a potential customer.

Interviewees also helped us translate vague benefits into concrete technical requirements. They said a viable solution must verify a person within roughly four to seven seconds so applicants do not abandon the process; run passively in the background so identity checks are not burdensome; reach high levels of accuracy to avoid the costs of false positives; sit at the front end of the identity verification process (or serve as a “step-up” check) to avoid unnecessary downstream verification costs; address privacy and consent concerns; and be delivered through an API or software development kit. We further learned that identity verification platforms value tools that create new revenue, not only those that reduce fraud losses, and that a typical sales path involves a nondisclosure agreement, developer access, and a two- to four-month proof-of-concept test against existing tools.

Of the 100 interviewees, 57 confirmed that deepfake fraud is a growing problem, that current detection tools are inadequate in both speed and accuracy, that existing tools can still be defeated by AI, and that they would pay up to $X per verification for an effective solution. Based on these findings, we estimate a total addressable market of $8.1 billion across all loan origination and identity verification calls, a serviceable market of $1.3 billion in alternative and specialty lending, and an obtainable market of $26 million at 2 percent penetration.

The team concluded that product-market fit exists and decided to launch a startup company. Over the next 12 months, we plan to run pilot and proof-of-concept tests with initial enterprise clients, build out compliance capabilities, improve our detection algorithms, integrate with additional clients, establish research partnerships, pursue seed funding and SBIR support, and continue customer discovery throughout.

Intellectual Merit: This project tested how research on human biometric and behavioral signals, grounded in media psychology, can be translated into a fast, accurate, and passive tool for distinguishing real people from AI-generated impostors. It produced a validated set of performance, integration, and privacy requirements that will guide further technical development.

Broader Impacts: Fraud losses raise costs for lenders and can reduce access to credit for borrowers who depend on online and alternative lending. Effective deepfake detection can protect consumers from identity theft, reduce financial losses, and strengthen trust in digital financial services. The project also built entrepreneurial capacity at Texas Tech University and contributes to the broader conversation on AI-enabled fraud.

Modified by: Eric   Rasmussen
